newsitem.title: USA: Regulators approve SBC, Pacific Telesis merger.
newsitem.headline: Regulators approve SBC, Pacific Telesis merger.

text.p: California regulators Monday approved SBC Communications Inc.'s $17 billion merger with Pacific Telesis Group on condition that customers receive a $341 million refund.

The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) was the only regulatory body whose approval of the merger was still required. The Federal Communications Commission approved the merger plan earlier this year.

The California commission, which voted 4-1 for the merger, said Pacific Telesis' Pacific Bell unit would issue the refund to customers over five years beginning in 1998 to reflect the short- and long-term economic benefits of the merger.
In present-value terms, the refund is worth about $248 million.
The directors of SBC, the parent of San Antonio, Texas-based Southwestern Bell, and Pacific Telesis plan to evaluate the commission's decision and decide whether to go through with the merger.
The final decision was sharply lower than the $590.5 million refund over five years proposed by two administrative law judges, who make recommendations to the commission.

SBC and San Francisco-based Pacific Telesis had urged the California commissioners to reject the judges' proposal and approve the merger without conditions, saying the benefits of the merger would flow to ratepayers in the form of lower prices for telecommunications services. They said the merger also would boost the California economy by creating new jobs.
Commissioners touted the economic benefits of the proposed merger, saying the combination of the two phone companies would boost the economy and provide jobs.
"This will afford California a significant opportunity," Commissioner Richard Bilas said. "There will be many beneficiaries: the merged companies, the ratepayers, (and the) stockholders."
Consumer groups had called for refunds to customers of nearly $1 billion over five years.
SBC and Pacific Telesis announced their merger plans last April. Shareholders from both companies approved the merger last summer.

The companies serve the nation's two most populous states -- California and Texas -- and seven of the nation's 10 largest metropolitan areas. Together, the two companies' 1996 revenues totalled $23.5 billion.
